k: Ibn Abbas (RA): the talbiyah of Umrah stops on touching the Black Stone. Your Hajj then has its own talbiyah, from the ihram on the {1}th until Jamrat al-Aqabah. Malikis stop the Umrah talbiyah on entering the Haram.
Ibn Majah {1} — and the Prophet ﷺ visited Quba every Saturday.
Ibn Majah {1} — drink it with a specific dua: knowledge, cure, forgiveness, whatever you need.
Ihram at the miqat, tawaf, sa'i, then cut the hair and leave ihram. You enter ihram again for Hajj on the {1}th.
Ihram, talbiyah, dhikr and dua all continue; only the tawaf (and its sa'i) wait for purity (Bukhari {1}).

Jabir (RA): the Prophet ﷺ and his companions — meaning those who, like him, stayed in ihram — went between Safa and Marwah only once: "his first tawaf." Hanafis hold that a Qiran pilgrim does a second sa'i; follow your school.
Ka'b ibn Ujrah was told: "Have your head shaved, then either fast three days, or feed six poor persons, or slaughter a sheep."
Labbayk Allahumma labbayk — "Here I am, O Allah, here I am," answering the call to pilgrimage.

Men walk briskly with short steps in rounds {1}–{2} of the tawaf of arrival — the Umrah tawaf, or tawaf al-qudum for Qiran and Ifrad. Hanafis and Shafi'is also do it in a later tawaf that is followed by sa'i (such as a Tamattu' pilgrim's tawaf al-ifadah); Hanbalis do not, and Malikis do so only for a pilgrim who did no arrival tawaf. Women walk normally.

On arrival he prayed Maghrib (three rakahs) and Isha (two) together, with no voluntary prayer between them, then lay down until dawn. Jabir (RA) reports one adhan and two iqamahs; Ibn Umar and Ibn Mas'ud (RA) describe the calls a little differently, and the schools follow different reports.

On the morning of the {1}th he said to Ibn Abbas, "Pick up some pebbles for me," and he told the people to take pebbles as he came into Muhassir. Many pick up seven at Muzdalifah; pebbles from anywhere will do — just not ones already thrown at the jamarat, which some schools do not count.

One adhan and two iqamahs (Muslim {1}), at Dhuhr time (Bukhari {2}), shortened to two rakahs each — then the standing begins. That is the Sunnah and majority practice; Abu Hanifa allowed combining only behind the imam, so many Hanafi groups pray each at its own time in the tents, and schools differ on who shortens — follow your group's scholar.
Only the big pillar (Aqabah) on the {1}th — seven pebbles, takbir with each (Bukhari {2}). All three are stoned on the {3}th–{4}th.
Only the big pillar, Jamrat al-Aqabah, on the {1}th — seven pebbles, a takbir with each. All three are stoned on the days that follow.
Qarn al-Manazil serves Najd, Taif and most eastern arrivals — be in ihram before the pilot's announcement.
Rawdah slots open only a short time ahead — check Nusuk as your dates approach and book as soon as they open.

Renew your wudu and return. Hanafis and Shafi'is build on the completed rounds (resume the interrupted round, or repeat it to be safe); Malikis and Hanbalis restart the tawaf from round {1}. Either way, no panic — nothing is ruined.

Renew your wudu and return. Hanafis and Shafi'is build on the rounds already done (resume the interrupted round, or repeat it to be safe); Malikis and Hanbalis restart from round {1} — the safer course if you are able. Nothing is lost either way.
Said to Amr ibn al-As (RA) when he accepted Islam and asked to be forgiven: "…and Hajj wipes out what came before it."
Sawdah left Muzdalifah early, and the Prophet ﷺ himself did tawaf mounted. Tawaf al-ifadah can be done late, on the upper floors or in a wheelchair — but never skipped.
Scented products are prohibited. Watches, glasses, belts and unscented showers are all fine.

Seven rounds in ordinary clothes, no raml and no sa'i; then the two rakahs prayed after every tawaf, and you leave. The Prophet ﷺ did his at night, after a short sleep at al-Muhassab, before setting out for Madinah.
Seven, one at a time, chickpea-sized — "beware of going to extremes" (Ibn Majah {1}).
Takbir with each pebble, then a long dua facing the qibla after the small and the middle — and none after Aqabah (Bukhari {1}).
Tamattu' — what the Prophet ﷺ told his companions without a sacrificial animal to do: tawaf, sa'i, cut the hair, leave ihram, then ihram for Hajj later. A hady is owed.

Tawaf al-ifadah is a pillar (Quran {1}): the Hajj stays incomplete until it is done. For the majority, the other three are wajibs, repaired by a dam if missed (Malikis count the farewell tawaf as sunnah).
Tawaf al-ifadah is a pillar: the Hajj stays incomplete until it is done. For the majority the other three are wajibs, repaired by a dam if missed (Malikis count the farewell tawaf a sunnah).

The Prophet ﷺ prayed Dhuhr to Fajr in Mina on the {1}th, and the four schools agree this stay is a sunnah — nothing is owed for missing it. Arafah and tawaf al-ifadah are pillars; the stoning is a wajib.
The Prophet ﷺ sent her with her brother Abdur-Rahman to Tan'eem: "This Umrah is instead of your missed one." Today Masjid Aisha stands there.
The congregation turned from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in a single prayer (Quran {1}).
The farewell tawaf: the last thing you do in Makkah before you travel home.
The izar wraps the lower body, the rida drapes the upper body — both unstitched.
The miqats are "for those who pass through them intending Hajj or Umrah" — on a plane, at the miqat announcement. Tamattu': ihram for Umrah; Qiran: for Umrah and Hajj; Ifrad: for Hajj.
The standing-stone of Ibrahim (AS) — "Take the Maqam of Ibrahim as a place of prayer." (Quran {1})
The words of tawhid — "None has the right to be worshipped but Allah alone, without partner; His is the dominion and His the praise, and He is over all things capable."
Three nights in Thawr — "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us." (Quran {1})
Tirmidhi {1} — and with every step a sin is erased and a good deed recorded.
True — "Had I not been driven out of you, I would never have left." (Tirmidhi {1})
True — "The jihad of the elderly, the young, the weak and women is Hajj and Umrah" (Nasai {1}); and to Aishah (RA): "jihad in which there is no fighting" (Ibn Majah {2}).
True — "Whoever is able to die in Madinah, let him die there, for I will intercede for him." (Tirmidhi {1})

True — "it is a part of the House" (Tirmidhi {1}): the part next to the Kaaba wall, roughly six cubits deep, lay inside the original Kaaba (Muslim {2}), so pray close to the wall. A rare chance most pilgrims miss!
True — "whoever hastens in two days there is no sin on him" (Quran {1}); for the majority, sunset inside Mina means staying for the {2}th.
True — "…and the sins of the children of Adam blackened it." (Tirmidhi {1})
True — "…as the bellows removes the dross of iron, gold and silver." (Tirmidhi {1})
True — "…there is no sexual relations and no disobedience and no disputing during Hajj." The manners of the pilgrim start the moment you enter ihram.
True — Abu Ayyub (RA) showed how the Prophet ﷺ washed his head while in ihram. Swapping a soiled set for a clean one is fine; only scented products are avoided.
True — Allah warns against "deviation to wrongdoing" in the Haram (Quran {1}). Guard your tongue and gaze doubly.

True — Ibn Umar (RA): "Whoever is at Mina when the sun sets on the middle day of tashreeq must not leave until he has stoned the jamarat the next day." The verse gives the choice — "whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin on him." Hanafis allow leaving that night, before Fajr of the {1}th; and many scholars, including Ibn Baz, excuse one who had already set off and was held up in Mina by the traffic.

True — Sawdah (RA), a slow woman, asked and he allowed her to leave before the rush; Ibn Abbas was sent ahead with the weak of the family. The schools differ on the earliest time (Shafi'is and Hanbalis: after midnight) — follow your group.
True — a belt is not fitted "stitched clothing"; it is how you keep your passport and cash safe.

True — a pillar is never "too late": the Hajj is completed when it is done. With an excuse such as a period, nothing is owed. Delaying it without an excuse is discouraged, and some schools then owe a dam (Hanafis, once the days of sacrifice have passed; Malikis, once Dhul Hijjah ends).

True — after her Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ sent Aishah (RA) with her brother to Tan'eem for an Umrah (Bukhari {1}, {2}). Most scholars allow it; Malikis dislike more than one Umrah a year, and some (e.g. Ibn Taymiyyah) prefer extra tawaf instead.
True — continue from where you left off. "Allah intends for you ease" (Quran {1}).
True — crossing your miqat without ihram when intending Umrah requires returning to it, or else, for most scholars, a dam (a sheep slaughtered in the Haram).

True — he declared sacred what lies between its two lava plains, as Ibrahim declared Makkah sacred (Muslim {1}). Most scholars forbid hunting and cutting its trees, though its rules are lighter than Makkah's; Hanafis do not give it Makkah's rulings.
True — one direction is one lap; seven laps finish on Marwah.
